prompt: What does CSMA/CA contribute to ordinary Wi-Fi operation?
options: Listening, waiting and backoff to reduce contention collisions
Full-duplex transmission and reception on the same ordinary radio
A dedicated collision-free channel for each associated station
Guaranteed retransmission-free delivery once a client associates
explanation: Carrier sensing and contention/backoff rules help stations share airtime. They do not eliminate collisions, retries or interference. Modern scheduling enhancements do not remove those basic RF limits.

whyWrong.1: The ordinary same-channel radio model here is half duplex.
whyWrong.2: Association does not allocate an independent radio channel per station.
whyWrong.3: Association is not a guarantee of error-free delivery.

prompt: For neighboring APs using the ordinary North American 2.4 GHz 20 MHz plan, which two statements are correct? Choose two.
options: A 40 MHz channel creates more independent frequency choices
Adjacent channel numbers have centers only 5 MHz apart
Channels 1, 2 and 3 provide three separate occupied ranges
Channels 1, 6 and 11 are the usual nonoverlapping reuse set
A different SSID lets nearby APs ignore shared airtime
explanation: Channel spacing is narrower than the occupied width. The usual 1/6/11 plan separates neighboring cells; increasing width consumes more spectrum.

whyWrong.0: Wider operation consumes spectrum rather than creating additional independent channels.
whyWrong.4: Different network names do not separate RF frequencies.

prompt: Why can an AP using a DFS-required 5 GHz channel leave that channel even when its clients have strong signals?
options: SSID uniqueness requires each AP to change its channel periodically
Radar protection requires it to vacate after a radar detection
A strong client signal causes a mandatory radio power shutdown
A WPA2 key renewal requires a different center frequency
explanation: DFS protects radar users of shared spectrum. Signal strength does not override the regulatory requirement; exact channels and timing depend on the deployment.

whyWrong.0: SSID uniqueness is not a DFS mechanism.
whyWrong.2: Strong signal alone does not cause the stated radar-driven behavior.
whyWrong.3: Security key renewal is separate from channel selection.

prompt: Wi-Fi 6E extends which radio technology into compatible 6 GHz equipment?
explanation: Wi-Fi 6E identifies the 6 GHz extension of 802.11ax. Both AP and client need compatible hardware and local regulatory support.

prompt: Which pairing is appropriate for the WPA2-PSK configuration taught in the CCNA GUI objective?
options: WPA2-Personal using AES-CCMP and a shared passphrase
WPA2-Enterprise using AES-CCMP and individual EAP credentials
WPA3-Personal using SAE and protected management frames
Original WPA-Personal using TKIP and a shared passphrase
explanation: The required WPA2-PSK exercise uses WPA2-Personal and AES-CCMP. WEP and TKIP are legacy choices, while WPA3 has its own authentication/security requirements.

whyWrong.1: That is an Enterprise authentication design, not the requested WPA2-PSK exercise.
whyWrong.2: That is WPA3-Personal rather than the stated WPA2-PSK setting.
whyWrong.3: Original WPA/TKIP is a legacy alternative, not this WPA2/AES exercise.

prompt: Which two statements describe a WPA3-Personal-only WLAN? Choose two.
options: It uses SAE for password-based authentication
It requires TKIP for compatibility with original WPA
It requires protected management frame support
It requires individual RADIUS accounts for every client
It removes the need to protect endpoints and credentials
explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE and requires PMF. These improve wireless protection but do not eliminate endpoint risks or all forms of radio disruption.

whyWrong.1: TKIP is obsolete and is not the WPA3-Personal cipher requirement.
whyWrong.3: Per-user 802.1X/RADIUS is an Enterprise design, not a Personal requirement.
whyWrong.4: Wireless security does not replace endpoint and credential protection.

exhibit.title: netsh wlan show interfaces — representative
exhibit.text:
State: connected
SSID: STAFF
Authentication: WPA2-Personal
Cipher: CCMP
Channel: 44
Receive rate (Mbps): 866.7

prompt: Which security interpretation is supported by the representative report?
options: The client is using an Enterprise EAP method against RADIUS
The client has completed a successful application throughput test
The connection uses TKIP because Personal mode requires RC4
The connection uses WPA2-Personal with the reported CCMP cipher
explanation: The Authentication and Cipher fields establish the reported WLAN security combination. They do not show an application performance test or prove end-to-end service access.

whyWrong.0: The report says Personal, not Enterprise.
whyWrong.1: A link-rate field is not a throughput measurement.
whyWrong.2: The reported cipher is CCMP, not TKIP.

exhibit.title: Windows-style scan — representative
exhibit.text:
SSID: STAFF
BSSID: 02:11:22:33:44:50   Band: 2.4 GHz   Channel: 6
BSSID: 02:11:22:33:44:51   Band: 5 GHz     Channel: 44

prompt: What can be concluded from this representative scan without consulting an AP inventory?
options: Two BSSIDs advertise STAFF; the scan does not establish physical ownership
The different bands require the clients to use two different network names
The two identifiers establish that both radios belong to one physical AP
The similar addresses establish that the second entry is a spoofed radio
explanation: One SSID can appear on multiple radios and APs. BSSID identifies the service set; similar MAC-style values do not establish which physical chassis owns them.

whyWrong.1: Different bands can advertise the same SSID.
whyWrong.2: Address similarity is not a verified physical inventory mapping.
whyWrong.3: A different or similar BSSID alone does not prove impersonation.

prompt: An AP changes from 20 dBm transmit power to 23 dBm. What is its approximate new power?
options: 50 mW
400 mW
200 mW
explanation: 20 dBm represents 100 mW. A 3 dB increase is approximately a doubling, giving about 200 mW; the exact value is about 199.5 mW.

whyWrong.0: About 50 mW corresponds to 17 dBm, a decrease.

prompt: At one receiver, signal is −65 dBm and noise is −92 dBm over the same observation period. What is SNR?
options: 27 dBm
−157 dBm
27 dB
−27 dB
explanation: Subtract noise from signal: −65 − (−92) = 27. SNR is a power ratio expressed in dB, not an absolute dBm level.

whyWrong.0: The numeric result is correct but the unit is not.
whyWrong.1: Adding the levels does not calculate SNR.

exhibit.title: Survey worksheet
exhibit.text:
AP-A: channel 1
AP-B: channel 6
AP-C: channel 6
AP-B and AP-C: strong mutual reception; high shared airtime utilization

prompt: All APs use 20 MHz in the North American 1/6/11 plan. The survey shows no other relevant channel-11 source. Which candidate change addresses the displayed reuse and should then be verified?
options: Move AP-C to channel 11 and verify the resulting RF behavior
Move AP-A to channel 6 so all APs can coordinate one channel
Move AP-B to channel 3 to separate it from AP-C numerically
Move AP-C to channel 8 to create a separate center frequency
explanation: The demonstrated problem is AP-B/AP-C sharing channel 6. Channel 11 is a suitable candidate in this stated plan; measurements after the change verify the result.

whyWrong.1: Adding another co-channel AP does not remove the existing contention.
whyWrong.2: Channel 3 introduces overlap rather than using the planned nonoverlapping set.
whyWrong.3: Channel 8 overlaps the neighboring channel-6 occupied spectrum.

exhibit.title: Verified deployment
exhibit.text:
AP1: SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:00:00:00:01:10
AP2: SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:00:00:00:02:10
Both bridge to VLAN 20 through the wired LAN.
The roaming client's address remains 10.20.0.57/24.

prompt: The managed deployment uses the same SSID and security on both APs with a common distribution system. What describes the combined service?
options: An independent basic service set
A single basic service set
An extended service set
A wireless mesh backhaul
explanation: The cooperating infrastructure BSSs form an ESS. The given shared VLAN supports this example's unchanged IP addressing, but identical SSIDs alone would not prove the same result.

whyWrong.0: An IBSS is an ad hoc arrangement without these infrastructure APs.
whyWrong.1: Each shown BSSID identifies a separate BSS.
whyWrong.3: The exhibit specifies wired distribution, not wireless mesh backhaul.

exhibit.title: Authorized diagnostic observations — authored worksheet
exhibit.text:
2.4 GHz client: strong received level, heavy retries while nearby microwave runs
Spectrum observation: non-Wi-Fi energy increases during operation
Controlled appliance off/on trials: impairment repeatedly disappears/returns
5 GHz comparison client: unaffected

prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the controlled observations?
options: The noon timing proves a neighboring AP changes channel
A DFS event on 2.4 GHz causes the recorded loss
The operating appliance is a demonstrated interference source
The laptop's strong signal rules out RF interference
explanation: The controlled repeated correlation and non-Wi-Fi energy measurement support the appliance as the source in this scenario. A lunchtime symptom alone would only suggest investigation.

whyWrong.0: No neighboring-AP channel change is shown.
whyWrong.1: The ordinary 2.4 GHz WLAN in this scenario does not use 5 GHz DFS.
whyWrong.3: Strong desired signal can coexist with interfering energy.

prompt: A WLAN design must support revoking one employee's individual credential. Which design directly meets that requirement?
options: Personal mode with one shared passphrase and MAC filtering
Personal mode with one periodically rotated staff passphrase
Personal mode with one shared passphrase and hidden SSID
Enterprise EAP with an individually managed account per employee
explanation: Individually managed Enterprise credentials allow targeted revocation. Enforcement can also require terminating existing sessions according to policy; disabling an account is not a promise that every active session ends instantly.

whyWrong.0: MAC filtering is not an individually authenticated credential and addresses can be copied.
whyWrong.1: Rotating a common secret affects the group rather than one employee's credential.
whyWrong.2: Hiding the SSID does not create individual authentication.

prompt: A surveyed point-to-point link needs a narrow beam aimed at a second building. Which listed pattern best matches that requirement?
options: An omnidirectional antenna covering the room horizontally
A directional dish with an 8-degree specified beamwidth
A broad wall-panel pattern covering a 120-degree sector
An omnidirectional ceiling pattern covering nearby desks
explanation: The stated narrow-beam dish fits the specified point-to-point coverage pattern. Actual suitability still depends on link budget, alignment, clearance and permitted power; antenna names or distance alone are insufficient.

whyWrong.0: Room-wide horizontal coverage does not match the requested narrow beam.
whyWrong.2: The supplied 120-degree sector is much broader than the stated link needs.
whyWrong.3: The supplied pattern is for local area coverage rather than the specified beam.

exhibit.title: Client status
exhibit.text:
Receive PHY rate: 600 Mb/s
Client count on shared channel: 24
Application file-transfer rate: not measured

prompt: Why does the reported PHY rate not establish a 600 Mb/s file-transfer rate?
options: Each associated client is reserved the displayed 600 Mb/s concurrently
The application rate is fixed at exactly half the displayed PHY rate
Changing the SSID isolates this client from the channel's other users
Overhead and shared airtime prevent that link rate from proving throughput
explanation: The link rate describes radio transmission capability for that connection. Useful application throughput depends on airtime, overhead, retries and the rest of the path; no fixed percentage applies universally.

whyWrong.0: The shared radio medium does not reserve the full link rate for every client.
whyWrong.1: There is no universal fixed PHY-to-application throughput ratio.
whyWrong.2: A network name does not create independent radio spectrum.

exhibit.title: Two RF measurements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Comparable readings at each client during the stated interval:
Client A: signal −54 dBm, noise −66 dBm
Client B: signal −66 dBm, noise −96 dBm
Application throughput has not been measured.

prompt: Which comparison is supported by the two measurements?
options: A has stronger signal and therefore must deliver higher throughput
A has 12 dBm SNR, while B has a weaker 30 dBm signal
B has 30 dB SNR, compared with A's 12 dB; throughput still needs testing
B must use a higher-power AP because its noise floor is lower
explanation: A: −54 − (−66) = 12 dB. B: −66 − (−96) = 30 dB. B has the better signal-to-noise ratio despite its weaker signal, but neither measurement alone guarantees application capacity.

whyWrong.0: Stronger desired signal can coexist with a much higher noise floor.
whyWrong.1: SNR is a ratio in dB; −66 dBm is B's received signal.
whyWrong.3: A lower noise floor does not establish the AP's transmit power.

exhibit.title: Bonded channel comparison (exercise)
exhibit.text:
AP-A: 5 GHz, 80 MHz width; occupied component channels 36, 40, 44 and 48.
AP-B: 5 GHz, 20 MHz width on channel 44.
The cells have strong mutual reception.

prompt: Which channel-width conclusion is correct?
options: Different primary channels prove the occupied spectrum is independent
The 80 MHz radio overlaps the narrower radio's channel spectrum
Renaming one SSID separates these transmissions in frequency
Both must have the same PHY rate because some spectrum overlaps
explanation: The supplied 80 MHz channel includes the component containing channel 44. Different primary-channel labels do not make their occupied spectrum disjoint. Channel width and the actual occupied range matter.

whyWrong.0: The primary-channel number does not describe the entire bonded range.
whyWrong.2: SSID naming does not change occupied frequencies.
whyWrong.3: Overlap does not determine equal rates; capabilities and conditions also matter.

exhibit.title: Measurement location and time (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Laptop receive level from AP-A: −60 dBm at 10:00.
AP-A noise floor: −95 dBm at 10:20 in a different location.
No laptop noise measurement is available.

prompt: Can these two readings establish the laptop's SNR?
options: No: obtain comparable signal and noise readings at the same receiver
Yes: subtract the distant AP's noise reading to obtain 35 dB
Yes: the shared SSID makes noise identical throughout the WLAN
No: negative dBm levels cannot be used in a subtraction
explanation: SNR compares desired signal with noise at the relevant receiver over a comparable interval and band. Combining a laptop's measurement with an AP's measurement elsewhere does not establish either receiver's SNR.

whyWrong.1: The arithmetic mixes different receivers and observation conditions.
whyWrong.2: The SSID does not make RF conditions uniform.
whyWrong.3: Negative dBm values are valid power levels; the issue is measurement comparability.

exhibit.title: Band compatibility requirements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Approved new WLAN: 6 GHz, WPA3-Personal.
Client vendor specification and driver report: 2.4/5 GHz only.
The business requires this client to retain authorized access; its current hardware has no 6 GHz upgrade path.

prompt: Which deployment change can meet the stated requirement without pretending a setting adds unsupported hardware?
options: Rename the 6 GHz SSID to match the client's saved 5 GHz profile
Provide an approved compatible band or replace/update to documented capable equipment
Select WPA2-only security on the 6 GHz radio for this client
Increase 6 GHz transmit power until the 5 GHz-only adapter can detect it
explanation: The verified client lacks a 6 GHz radio capability. Use a supported, approved band for it or obtain equipment with documented 6 GHz support. A name, power change or security downgrade cannot add the missing radio band.

whyWrong.0: SSID equality does not add a radio capability.
whyWrong.2: WPA2-only is not the appropriate 6 GHz security design and would not add band support.
whyWrong.3: Increasing power does not change the adapter's supported frequency band.

exhibit.title: A direction-specific RF change (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Same stationary client before/after an approved AP power increase:
Client receives AP: −72 -> −61 dBm.
AP receives client: −81 -> −81 dBm; uplink retries remain high.
Security completes; client address/gateway are correct.
Downloads improve, uploads still fail the application acceptance test.

prompt: Which next action best addresses the evidence without assuming more AP power fixes both directions?
options: Raise the AP power again because the client hears it well
Inspect client-to-AP coverage and placement using repeated two-direction tests
Replace the DHCP pool because association implies good radio delivery
Widen the channel before checking the weak client-to-AP path
explanation: The AP's higher transmit power improved only what the client receives. The AP still hears a weak client transmission and uplink retries remain high. Investigate placement, obstructions and client capability in that direction, then compare the same tests before claiming recovery.

whyWrong.0: Further AP transmit power does not increase the client's transmit capability.
whyWrong.2: The supplied valid addressing and directional RF evidence do not identify a DHCP fault.
whyWrong.3: More width does not establish a repair for the weak return radio path.

exhibit.title: Roaming and retained addressing (exercise)
exhibit.text:
AP-A and AP-B advertise STAFF with the same approved security.
Client was on AP-A/VLAN 20 with 10.20.0.57/24, gateway 10.20.0.1.
After moving: BSSID maps to AP-B; security succeeds; signal is strong.
The old IP settings remain, but the gateway and application no longer respond.
AP-B's wired VLAN/mobility mapping has not been verified.

prompt: Which next check best separates the wireless identity from the broken IP path?
options: Treat the shared SSID as proof that both BSSIDs lead to VLAN 20
Raise the client signal threshold because strong RSSI proves DHCP succeeded
Change the server's address because a changed BSSID proves a server fault
Check AP-B's forwarding/VLAN design and the client's valid subnet after the move
explanation: The client changed cells and completed compatible security, but the retained address is not automatically correct behind AP-B. Verify the authorized mapping/mobility design and obtain valid addressing for that path. Same SSID and good signal do not establish the same VLAN or uninterrupted sessions.

whyWrong.0: SSID equality is not proof of an identical wired forwarding domain.
whyWrong.1: Signal strength does not prove a fresh DHCP exchange or correct subnet.
whyWrong.2: No supplied evidence identifies a server addressing change.

exhibit.title: Two plausible interference explanations (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Lunchtime calls deteriorate on 2.4 GHz; signal stays strong.
Scan shows nearby APs; retries increase, but utilization and spectrum were not recorded.
A microwave is nearby, and client load also rises at lunchtime.
Security and IP settings remain valid.

prompt: Which next test would best distinguish the proposed RF causes?
options: Declare the nearby microwave responsible because loss happens at lunch
Replace the shared passphrase because channel scans cannot show passwords
Change every AP to the strongest scanned channel and compare afterward
Record band, retries/utilization and spectrum during controlled authorized comparisons
explanation: The symptoms suggest investigation but do not identify one source. Correlate comparable RF and service evidence, and use an authorized controlled change that separates the suspected non-Wi-Fi source from competing Wi-Fi load. Change one factor at a time.

whyWrong.0: Timing and proximity alone do not establish the cause.
whyWrong.1: No supplied security failure is shown, and password changes do not diagnose RF load.
whyWrong.2: The strongest scanned signal does not identify the least congested channel; changing every AP loses experimental control.
